Andrew Thomson
an'droo tom'sən
n. (Andrew Mitchell Thomson, 1779–1831, minister of St George's, Edinburgh, leader of the Apocrypha controversy and of immediate abolition)
Greek Andreas, manly; Scottish patronymic Thom-son, son of Thomas.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Andrew Thomson was minister of St George's, Edinburgh, from 1814, editor of the Christian Instructor, and the dominant evangelical voice in the Church of Scotland in the generation before the Disruption. Two controversies made him. In the first he discovered that the British and Foreign Bible Society was circulating Bibles on the continent with the Apocrypha bound in and interspersed among the canonical books, and he fought the practice until the Society resolved to circulate the canonical Scriptures alone; the Edinburgh Bible Society separated over it. In the second he broke with the gradualists of the anti-slavery movement and argued for immediate and total emancipation, on the ground that a thing forbidden by God is not to be phased out on a timetable. He died suddenly at fifty-two, and his pulpit passed in time to Candlish. Deu 4:2 is the Apocrypha argument, and Exo 21:16 the other.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines apocrypha as books whose authors are not known, not admitted into the sacred canon, and canon as a rule, the genuine books of Scripture.

expand to see more

APOC'RYPHA, n. Books whose authors are not known; books appended to the sacred Scriptures, but being of doubtful origin, are not esteemed canonical.

CAN'ON, n. In an ecclesiastical sense, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline; the genuine books of the Holy Scriptures, called the sacred canon.

EMANCIPA'TION, n. The act of setting free from servitude or slavery; deliverance from bondage.

Key Scripture

Deu 4:2 — "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you."

Rev 22:18 — "For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:"

Exo 21:16 — "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death."

Isa 58:6 — "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?"

Modern Corruption

He got the Apocrypha out of the Bible Society's Bibles and refused a timetable for emancipation.

expand to see more

The Apocrypha controversy looks like a quarrel over bookbinding and is a question about the canon. A Bible in which Tobit and Maccabees stand between Nehemiah and Esther teaches the reader, without a word of argument, that these books have the same standing as the rest. Deu 4:2 forbids adding to the word that God commanded, and Rev 22:18 pronounces the warning at the other end of the canon. Thomson was accused of harshness toward a benevolent society; he was defending the sixty-six books.

On slavery his position was the one the dictionary holds and the one most of his contemporaries would not take. Gradual emancipation treats a sin as an institution to be wound down; Exo 21:16 fixes a capital penalty on manstealing, and Isa 58:6 commands the loosing of the bands of wickedness, to “let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6), with no clause allowing for a transitional period. The corruption to name is the respectable moderation that grants a wrong is a wrong and then schedules its end for a generation that will not have to pay for it.

Usage

"“Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you” (Deu 4:2) — the Apocrypha argument."

"“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — why not gradually."

"“let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6) — no transitional clause."
